Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson (Strategy Data Pack, Friday) says the S&P 500 “catching down” to weaker breadth “is likely the final stage of this correction," after he rightly called a continuation of the pullback in semi's in the event of a big Democratic victory.

But he isn’t calling the bottom yet: “We are getting close, but would like to see… further confirmation from our sentiment indicator.” His year-end target stays 8,000.

Here's what’s happened to the three “clearing events” he laid out last weekend:

▪️ Midterms: Democrats took both chambers, with at least 54 Senate seats. Wilson had said a 52-48 Senate was priced in but 55-45 wasn’t, and that a bigger margin could fuel pushback on data centers, so he nailed that.
▪️ AI and semis: Thursday was the S&P’s worst day since April 2025 (−4.4%) and the Nasdaq-100’s worst since March 2020 (−6.4%). The SOX fell about 12% on weak chip guidance and fears of data-center rules after the election. That left it down about 19% from October 26, when Wilson called for another 10% to 15% drop into mid-November, another hit.
▪️ Liquidity, the one he ranks most important, hasn’t cleared. He says Fed Chair Warsh acknowledged financial conditions are doing some of the Fed’s tightening but wouldn’t call them “tight,” so the bar for a dovish pivot “remains high.” Then Friday’s payrolls (+165,000 vs. ~65,000 expected) pushed December hike odds to about 78%.

The math from Friday’s close of 7,376.86 (−5.7% from the record, −2.7% on the week):
▪️ 7,100 to 7,200 is another 2.4% to 3.8% down.
▪️ 8,000 is +8.4% from here. His 12-month base case is 8,300 (+12.5%), with a 5,900 bear case and 9,400 bull case.

On the catch-down, as he also indicated was likely, the average stock is holding up better than the index:
▪️ Thursday, the equal-weight S&P fell 2.9% vs. 4.4% for the cap-weighted index.
▪️ In October, equal-weight beat cap-weight by 5.9 points, the second-widest monthly gap since 2003.
▪️ Wilson notes median Russell 3000 earnings growth is running 14%, the strongest in four years.

His sentiment indicator was at −0.75 as of Thursday. That compares with roughly −1.45 at the Iran-war low earlier this year and about −2.1 on Liberation Day.

As always, a nice update from Eric who remains bullish long term on the AI trade: 

"Remember Liberation Day? Remember the DeepSeek scare? Both caused panic. Both looked like the end of the AI trade at the time. Look where we are since then.

"The AI revolution isn’t collapsing. This is a speed bump."

He also notes that historically after large VIX spikes "Fear spikes. Then it fades. The market has a habit of rewarding those who don’t panic."

In that regard has he some stats on VIX spikes, but we also had an even more notable spike in the VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) which saw its biggest one-day percentage gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon in 2018.

We’ve had six cases since 2007 of the VIX rising at least 40% and the VVIX at least 30% on the same day. The S&P 500 was higher a month later in all six, by an average of 2.3%. At three months, though, only four of the six were higher, by an average of 2.3%. That’s no better than the S&P 500’s typical three-month gain since 2007, about 2.5%, which was higher 72% of the time, but is certainly not bear market material.

The outliers were October 10, 2018, and November 26, 2021. The October 2018 spike came as rising Treasury yields and the Fed’s hawkish push (it was a week before Powell's infamous “a long way from neutral" statement) hit tech stocks. It turned out to be the start of the fourth-quarter selloff, which took the S&P 500 down almost 20% by Christmas Eve, and the index was 6.8% lower three months later.

Late Friday we got the Fed's US consumer credit report for September which showed a jump of $27.84 billion, the most since November 2022. That’s about double the $13.80 billion expected and above every estimate in Bloomberg’s survey with both revolving (mostly credit cards) and nonrevolving debt seeing double-digit increases.

▪️ Revolving (mostly credit cards) rose $16.30 billion (+14.46% annualized), the most since November 2023. That came a month after August’s drop, which was revised down to $4.97 billion and was the biggest decline since November 2024.
▪️ Nonrevolving (mostly student and auto loans) rose $11.54 billion. That brings its three-month total to $39.63 billion, the most since December 2022.
▪️ All three measures are at record highs: total $5.224 trillion, revolving $1.368 trillion and nonrevolving $3.856 trillion.
▪️ Year-over-year, revolving is up 4.25%, the fastest since October 2024. Total is up 3.01% and nonrevolving 2.57%.
▪️ The Fed’s quarterly detail shows student loans ($1.885 trillion) and auto loans ($1.590 trillion) both at records at the end of September.
▪️ The rate on credit card accounts assessed interest rose to 22.36% in the third quarter, the highest since August 2025, from 22.15%.

Bloomberg frames this as consumers leaning on cards because real pay is lagging prices. Hourly earnings are up 3.12% from a year ago, while September CPI was 3.7%.

But zooming out after inflation (September CPI 3.7%), total consumer credit is down 0.69% from a year ago, the seventh straight month below zero, and card balances are up only about half a point, versus more than 8% in late 2022. August and September together added $11.33 billion in card balances, or $5.67 billion a month. That’s only a bit above the past year’s $4.64 billion monthly average, so September is more catch-up. 

Also keep in mind these are balances at a single point in time during the monthly cycle, and much of them gets paid off before any interest is charged.
